steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on ID-like prompt learning for few-shot out-of-distribution detection with CLIP. Explain why OOD detection matters, what is wrong with existing approaches (ID-only training, auxiliary outliers, virtual outlier synthesis), how we construct ID-like outliers and learn extra prompts for them, and list our contributions.

  - Fig. 2 right: "dog-like" prompt; dogs via "dog", challenging OOD (incl. "wolf") via "dog-like"

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
When machine learning models are deployed in practice, they may come across out-of-distribution (OOD) samples that were not seen during training. For these OOD inputs the risk of wrong decisions is higher, which could cause serious safety issues, especially in applications like autonomous driving and medical diagnosis. To make trustworthy predictions, the system has to identify OOD samples as well as perform well on ID samples. So OOD detection is very critical for deploying machine learning models safely in reality.

Existing methods usually detect OOD examples using only ID data in training, and predict lower confidence or higher energy for OOD samples. But since they lack OOD information, these models struggle to be effective in OOD detection. So some studies suggest using auxiliary outliers to regularize the models and identify OOD samples. Other works suggested that choosing more challenging outlier samples can help the model learn a better decision boundary between ID and OOD. However, these limited auxiliary outliers contain even fewer challenging outliers. Also, most of these methods need additional outlier data, so they do not work when outlier datasets are not available. Recently, another work proposed a method that synthesizes virtual outlier data from the low-likelihood region in the feature space of ID data, so that outliers are constructed during training without additional data. This method is strongly effective at distinguishing ID and OOD. But it has two main limitations: i) it assumes ID data in the feature space follows a class conditional Gaussian distribution, which does not always hold in complex real-world applications; ii) it needs many ID samples to construct a more accurate distribution of ID data, and getting a large number of ID samples is often costly. So in this work we focus on constructing informative outliers in a flexible way to improve the identification of challenging OOD samples.

  - outliers highly correlated with ID data; novel ID-like prompts
  - challenging OOD samples: high visual/semantic similarity to ID, e.g. local feature relevant to ID (Fig. 1)
  - idea: extract relevant features from ID samples to build challenging OOD
  - multiple samplings in vicinity space of ID samples
  - samplings with lower similarity to ID prompts -> not ID classes despite ID-correlated features -> challenging OOD
  - unlike VOS and NPOS (low-likelihood feature regions): from original images; flexibility, interpretability
- ID-like prompts
  - identifying constructed OOD still hard
  - Fig. 2 left: "wolf" challenging OOD for "dog"; similar to ID prompts, high classification probability
  - ID prompts alone insufficient -> additional prompts
  - Fig. 2 right: "dog-like" prompt; dogs via "dog", challenging OOD (incl. "wolf") via "dog-like"
  - align additional prompts with constructed OOD -> OOD prompts similar to ID prompts
  - superior few-shot OOD detection, many real-world tasks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
When machine learning models are deployed in practice, they may come across out-of-distribution (OOD) samples that were not seen during training. For these OOD inputs the risk of wrong decisions is higher, which could cause serious safety issues, especially in applications like autonomous driving and medical diagnosis. To make trustworthy predictions, the system has to identify OOD samples as well as perform well on ID samples. So OOD detection is very critical for deploying machine learning models safely in reality.

Existing methods usually detect OOD examples using only ID data in training, and predict lower confidence or higher energy for OOD samples. But since they lack OOD information, these models struggle to be effective in OOD detection. So some studies suggest using auxiliary outliers to regularize the models and identify OOD samples. Other works suggested that choosing more challenging outlier samples can help the model learn a better decision boundary between ID and OOD. However, these limited auxiliary outliers contain even fewer challenging outliers. Also, most of these methods need additional outlier data, so they do not work when outlier datasets are not available. Recently, another work proposed a method that synthesizes virtual outlier data from the low-likelihood region in the feature space of ID data, so that outliers are constructed during training without additional data. This method is strongly effective at distinguishing ID and OOD. But it has two main limitations: i) it assumes ID data in the feature space follows a class conditional Gaussian distribution, which does not always hold in complex real-world applications; ii) it needs many ID samples to construct a more accurate distribution of ID data, and getting a large number of ID samples is often costly. So in this work we focus on constructing informative outliers in a flexible way to improve the identification of challenging OOD samples.

In this paper, we first construct outliers that are highly correlated with ID data, and introduce novel ID-like prompts for OOD detection, so that challenging OOD samples are identified effectively. We find that challenging OOD samples are often highly correlated with ID data and have high visual or semantic similarity, e.g., the local feature of OOD is relevant to ID (as shown in Fig. 1). These ID-like features of OOD samples lead to wrong predictions, so a natural idea is to extract relevant features from ID samples to construct challenging OOD samples. To do this, we perform multiple samplings on the vicinity space of ID samples. Among these samplings, the ones with lower similarity to the ID prompts are not classified as ID classes, even though they contain features correlated with ID classes. So these samples are naturally selected as challenging OOD samples. Unlike VOS and NPOS, which synthesize virtual outliers in low-likelihood regions of the feature space, our method constructs outliers directly from the original images, which makes it more flexible and interpretable.

Even though we can construct challenging OOD samples, identifying them effectively is still challenging. In the left part of Fig. 2, “ wolf ” is a challenging OOD example of the “ dog ” class. These images are similar to the ID prompts, so they get high classification probabilities, which makes it very hard to distinguish ID and OOD. We think relying only on ID prompts is not enough to solve this. So we introduce additional prompts to improve OOD identification. In the right part of Fig. 2, we develop an additional prompt called “ dog-like ”, which is similar to the “ dog ” prompt. If the similarity between the “ dog-like ” prompt and the OOD samples highly correlated with “ dog ” can be increased, then the model would recognize dogs through the “ dog ” prompt and identify challenging OOD samples (including “ wolf ”) through the “ dog-like ” prompt. Specifically, we align the additional prompts with the constructed challenging OOD, which creates OOD prompts similar to ID prompts to identify challenging OOD samples effectively. Extensive experiments show that our method gets superior few-shot OOD detection performance on many real-world tasks. Compared to methods that need a large amount of data in training, our method reduces the average FPR95 score from 38.24% to 24.08% and improves the average AUROC from 91.60% to 94.70%, even when only one image is used for each class. Our main contributions are:

- • We propose a novel framework without additional training that uses CLIP to automatically explore ID-like OOD samples in the vicinity space of ID samples, which helps the model identify challenging OOD samples correlated to the ID.

- • Using the capacity of a pre-trained visual-language model, we propose an ID-like prompt learning method to identify the most challenging OOD samples, which behave ID-like but are distinct.

- • We validated our method on several large-scale datasets, and it achieved impressive performance, with an average AUROC of 96.66% in 4-shot OOD detection on ImageNet-1K. We also do additional ablation experiments to show the effectiveness of the approach.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
When deploying machine learning models in practical settings, it is possible to come across out-of-distribution (OOD) samples that were not encountered during training. The risk of incorrect decisions rises for these OOD inputs, which could pose serious safety issues, particularly in applications like autonomous driving and medical diagnosis. To produce trustworthy predictions, the system needs to identify OOD samples in addition to performing well on ID samples. OOD detection is therefore critical for safely deploying machine learning models in reality.

Existing methods [1,2,3] usually focus on detecting OOD examples using only ID data in training, predicting lower confidence [4,5] or higher energy [6] for OOD samples. However, due to the lack of OOD information, these models struggle to be effective in OOD detection. Therefore, some studies [6,7] suggest using auxiliary outliers to regularize the models and identify OOD samples. [8] and [9] suggested that selecting more challenging outlier samples can help the model learn a better decision boundary between ID and OOD. However, these limited auxiliary outliers contain even fewer challenging outliers. Furthermore, most of these methods require additional outlier data, which makes them ineffective when outlier datasets are unavailable. Recently, [10] proposed to synthesize virtual outlier data from the low-likelihood region in the feature space of ID data, constructing outliers during training without additional data. This method is highly effective in distinguishing between ID and OOD, but it has two main limitations: i) it assumes that ID data in the feature space conforms to a class conditional Gaussian distribution, which does not always hold in complex real-world applications [11]; ii) it requires numerous ID samples to construct an accurate distribution of ID data, while obtaining a large number of ID samples is often costly. Accordingly, in this work we focus on flexibly constructing informative outliers to improve the identification of challenging OOD samples.

In this paper, we first construct outliers highly correlated with ID data and introduce novel ID-like prompts for OOD detection, thereby effectively identifying challenging OOD samples. We find that challenging OOD samples are often highly correlated with ID data, exhibiting high visual or semantic similarity, e.g., the local feature of OOD being relevant to ID (as shown in Fig. 1). Since these ID-like features of OOD samples lead to erroneous predictions, a natural idea arises: extracting relevant features from ID samples to construct challenging OOD samples. To this end, we perform multiple samplings on the vicinity space of ID samples. Among these samplings, those with lower similarity to the ID prompts are not classified as ID classes, even though they contain features correlated with ID classes, so they are naturally selected as challenging OOD samples. Unlike VOS [10] and NPOS [11], which synthesize virtual outliers in low-likelihood regions of the feature space, our method constructs outliers directly from the original images, enhancing flexibility and interpretability.

Although we can construct challenging OOD samples, it is still difficult to identify them effectively. As shown in the left part of Fig. 2, “ wolf ” represents a challenging OOD example of the “ dog ” class. These images are similar to ID prompts, resulting in high classification probabilities and making it hard to distinguish between ID and OOD. We argue that relying solely on ID prompts is insufficient, and therefore introduce additional prompts to enhance OOD identification. As shown in the right part of Fig. 2, we develop an additional prompt, termed “ dog-like ”, which is similar to the “ dog ” prompt. If we can increase the similarity between the “ dog-like ” prompt and OOD samples highly correlated with “ dog ”, the model would recognize dogs through the “ dog ” prompt and identify challenging OOD samples (including “ wolf ”) through the “ dog-like ” prompt. Specifically, we align the additional prompts with the constructed challenging OOD, creating OOD prompts similar to ID prompts to effectively identify challenging OOD samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior few-shot OOD detection performance on a wide variety of real-world tasks. Compared to methods [11,10] that require a large amount of training data, our method reduces the average FPR95 score from 38.24% to 24.08% and improves the average AUROC from 91.60% to 94.70%, even using only one image per class. We summarize our main contributions as follows:

- • We propose a novel framework without additional training that leverages CLIP to automatically explore ID-like OOD samples in the vicinity space of ID samples, helping the model effectively identify challenging OOD samples correlated to the ID.

- • By exploiting the capacity of a pre-trained visual-language model, we propose an ID-like prompt learning method to identify the most challenging OOD samples, which behave ID-like yet are distinct.

- • We validated our method on several large-scale datasets, and the results show impressive performance, with an average AUROC of 96.66% in 4-shot OOD detection on ImageNet-1K. Additional ablation experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the designed approach.
